Alright folks, let’s talk about Roy Williams, a remarkable jazz trombonist from England. He was born on March 7, 1937, in Salford, and you won't believe this—he didn’t even pick up the trombone until he was 18! Can you imagine diving into something new at that age?

Now, before that, he started out learning the piano when he was a kid, but then he served in the military during the late 1950s. Once he got out, he jumped into the jazz scene, initially joining a trad jazz group led by Mike Peters. Fast forward to the early 60s, and he was playing with Terry Lightfoot, which was no small feat!

By 1965, Roy became part of Alex Welsh's band, and that’s where things really took off. He shared the stage with jazz legends like Ruby Braff, Wild Bill Davison, and Bud Freeman. He stuck with Welsh until 1978 and even teamed up with his bandmate John Barnes for some side projects along the way.

After that, from 1978 to 1983, he joined Humphrey Lyttelton's ensemble, and in 1980, he was also playing with the Pizza Express All Stars and Benny Waters. So, he was really busy making connections and showcasing his talent!

When he wrapped up with Lyttelton in 1983, he didn’t slow down at all. Throughout the 80s and 90s, he became a familiar face at jazz festivals, working alongside some incredible musicians like Doc Cheatham, Jim Galloway, and Buddy Tate, just to name a few.

So, there you have it! Roy Williams is a quintessential figure in the jazz world, and his journey is a fantastic testament to following your passion and making it in the music industry.

Alright, everyone, let’s dive into the vibrant world of Cambodian entertainment! Today, I want to share a look at some of the key players in the film industry over the years.

So, first up, let's talk about the companies that really shaped the scene after the Khmer Rouge fell. It’s fascinating to see how this industry has evolved!

We kick things off with the 1960s, where we have TVK, or Khmer Television, which began back in 1966. Fun fact: it was Cambodia’s original broadcasting station and stuck to black and white broadcasts all the way until 1986! That’s a long time before the colorful world we enjoy today.

Moving into the 70s, we’ve got Pisnoka, founded in 1970 and owned by the popular actor Vann Vannak. If you were a fan of his, you’d notice he played the leading role in every single film they made until 1975. Then, there's Sovann Kiri, which ran from 1972 to 1984. This was a unique Khmer-Thai joint film company run by movie stars Dy Saveth and Hui Keung, and they had quite the journey, operating in Cambodia before taking their show to Hong Kong.

Then we jump to the 1980s, and another notable name arises: CM International Film, which has been around since 1985 and is owned by Sem Sovandeth. 

Fast forward to the 1990s, and we see a burst of creativity with companies like Angkorwat Films, started by Yvette Som, and Reksmey Hang Meas, both kicking off in 1990. Let's not forget SM, also founded in 1990 and run by Mai Sameth. It was a thriving time for the industry!

And let’s not skip over the 2000s, when Khmer Entertainment Inc. launched in 2005, led by CEO Lim Cheang. This company really focuses on promoting entertainment for Cambodian Americans and has been instrumental in hosting big performances across various US cities.

Now, let’s spotlight some of the talented individuals behind the camera! For instance, Fey Som Ang, who’s been a significant figure since 1989, is a renowned Cambodian film director, and he’s also worked on some Thai productions. Then there's Parn Puong Bopha, who has been making waves as a director since the same year!

So there you have it, a snapshot of the amazing companies and talented people making their mark in Cambodia's film and entertainment landscape. It’s a rich history filled with creativity and resilience, and it’s only getting better!

Let’s talk about Tesco Bank. So, it’s a British retail bank that started out way back in July 1997, originally known as Tesco Personal Finance. Since 2008, Tesco plc has owned it completely. It all began as a partnership with The Royal Bank of Scotland — a 50:50 joint venture, actually. You know, Tesco is the biggest supermarket in the UK, so they definitely had a strong foundation.

As time went on, Tesco decided it was a good move to buy out RBS's stake, making Tesco Bank a fully owned subsidiary. This means it operates under its own banking license now, and it’s part of the Financial Services Compensation Scheme—so there’s some peace of mind for customers.

What does Tesco Bank offer? A whole bunch of services, actually! They have insurance, credit cards, loans, savings options, mortgages, and even travel products. In June 2014, they added current accounts to their lineup.

One of the cool things about Tesco Bank is how they use their huge customer base to sell their financial products. If you’re a Tesco shopper, you can earn Tesco Clubcard points when you purchase their financial products. So, it's a nice little perk there. In fact, Tesco Bank recently ranked third in the British Bank Awards, boasting an impressive customer satisfaction rating of 87.8%. 

As for a bit of history, before Tesco Personal Finance was born, there was actually a banking joint venture with NatWest, but that ended back in February 1997. Then, just a few months later, in July, Tesco launched their own banking venture, riding the wave of success from some competitors like Sainsbury's Bank. So there you have it!

Alright, let’s talk about Nedim Halilović. He was born on July 1, 1979, in Brčko, and he’s a retired international football player from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Alright, let’s dive into "Next Is the E," or as some of you might know it, "I Feel It." This catchy tune is from Moby, an American electronic musician, and it first hit the airwaves back in October 1992. It was actually the third single from his self-titled debut album.

So, the release date? Mark your calendars for October 28, 1992. The song did pretty well on the charts, making it all the way up to number eight on the Billboard Hot Dance Music/Club Play chart. Plus, if you're a fan of '90s films, you might recognize it from the soundtrack of "Cool World."

Pretty cool, right? Let's keep the vibe going!

Alright folks, let’s chat a bit about Cachoeira Paulista! This little gem is a municipality in Brazil, nestled in the state of São Paulo. It’s part of the Metropolitan Region of Vale do Paraíba e Litoral Norte, specifically in the Guaratinguetá Microregion.

Now, if you’re looking for it on a map, you’ll find it at about 22 degrees south latitude and 45 degrees west longitude, sitting pretty at an altitude of 521 meters. As of 2017, the town had around 32,773 residents.

Cachoeira Paulista shares borders with a few other cities: to the north, there’s Cruzeiro; east is Silveiras; south and west, you’ll find Lorena; and to the southwest, it’s Canas. 

And here’s a fun fact! Cachoeira Paulista is home to the Brazilian Decimetric Array radio telescope, which is pretty cool for those interested in astronomy. Plus, part of the municipality lies in the Mananciais do Rio Paraíba do Sul Environmental Protection Area, which was established back in 1982 to help protect the river’s sources.

Now, let's take a little trip back in time. The history of Cachoeira Paulista dates back to 1730 when it was just a settlement within the Village of Lorena. They called it the Arraial of the Porto da Caxoeira. It all began with a small hermitage built by some devoted folks in honor of Lord Bom Jesus da Cana Verde in 1780. Then, on October 18, 1784, a couple named Manoel da Silva Caldas and his wife Ângela Maria de Jesus made a generous donation of land, specifically a stretch that was two fathoms wide and half a mile long on the left bank of the Paraíba River.

Isn’t that fascinating?

Alright, let’s dive into the Greene Naftali Gallery—an exciting spot in Chelsea, New York City, where contemporary art is the star of the show.

Fast forward to 1995, and Carol took the plunge to open her own place, Greene Naftali. She doesn’t just run this gallery; she’s also deeply involved in various arts organizations, like Artists Space, where she’s on the board. And fun fact—she shares her life with talented artist Craig Kalpakjian in NYC.

The gallery showcases a mix of contemporary art across different media. You’ll find everything from painting to video, and even music and fashion! What’s cool is that they have a knack for highlighting emerging artists, alongside some historical heavyweights like Rachel Harrison and Paul Chan.

But that’s not all. Greene Naftali is also known for its ambitious performance programming. They’ve welcomed a fantastic lineup of musicians and performers, including names like Thurston Moore and Dan Graham. So, whether you’re an art lover or just someone looking for a unique experience, this gallery is definitely a must-visit!
